newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan leaders tackle island's post-Deng security.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan leaders tackle island's post-Deng security.

text.p: A top-level security panel met on Monday to discuss implications for Taiwan's security following the death of China's Deng Xiaoping, who personified Beijing's zeal to retake the Nationalist-ruled island.
"We had a wide airing of opinions (about the situation in post-Deng China)," a tight-lipped Chang King-yuh, Taiwan's top China policymaker, said after the closed-door meeting.

"We exchanged views on possible changes in the mainland leadership, its political and economic direction, social situation and ethnic minorities and the relationship between local and central governments," he said.
Chang said Deng's death was a central focus but not the only topic discussed by the ad hoc security and stabilisation task force, comprising the cabinet and all security agencies.

The body was formed during the last big crisis to roil the Taiwan strait -- China's mounting months of threatening missile tests and war games near Taiwan after the island's president angered Beijing with an unofficial U.S. visit in June 1995.
Chang said Deng's passing had caused few ripples in Taiwan.
"So far our (Taiwan) compatriots have dealt with this issue calmly," he said. "After all, this is something that happened on the mainland. So we haven't felt any particular effect."
The task force has reconvened periodically to set policy towards communist China, which sees Taiwan as a renegade province that eventually must be brought under mainland rule.
Communist Beijing and Nationalist Taipei have remained bitter rivals since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
Deng himself placed top priority on bringing Taiwan under the communist red flag, urging it to accept the "one country, two systems" model now being pioneered in Hong Kong.
Taiwan has flatly refused, saying China must open up its political system before reunicaation can be considered.

Taiwan appealed to the world on Sunday not to lose sight of the fact that despite Deng's death one part of China -- Taiwan -- remained under the sovereignty of the exiled Republic of China government, not the communists.
"There is one divided China," a government statement said. "Neither Taipei nor Beijing governs the other side. Therefore, neither side can say it represents all of China."

Analysts said Taiwan was determined not to let Deng's death alter the delicate balance under which the economies of Taiwan and China have become increasingly interdependent despite a conspicuous lack of official or informal contacts.
With U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Beijing on Monday, Taipei was watching closely for any signs of further warming of U.S.-China ties that might come at Taiwan's expense.

Washington has given dramatic support for Taiwan's fledgling democracy despite having diplomatic relations only with China. It sent two aircraft carriers to the region during the March 1996 missile crisis in an unambiguous warning to Beijing.
A nervous Taiwan appealed openly on Saturday for Washington to balance its Taiwan and China ties by providing better weapons to Taiwan to counter any possible threat from Beijing.

"We call for a parallel development of relations," Taiwan's de facto Washington ambassador said. "When (the United States) improves ties with the Chinese communists, it must at the same time upgrade the level of (relations) with us."
Taiwan's defence minister said a first batch of anti-missile U.S. Patriot missiles were already being deployed.
Taiwan also worries over its economic vulnerability.

After Deng's death, Taipei called on investors to approach the China market with caution, warning anew that Taiwan must not allow itself to become dangerously over-reliant on the increasingly alluring economy of its only adversary.

China's government -- which suspects President Lee Teng-hui is manoeuvring to create a sovereign Taiwan republic despite publicly espousing eventual reunification -- reserves the right to take the island by force if it seeks formal independence.
